elements.char: volatility pricing the same as any other pricing exercise. Second, we do not have to assume a
elements.label: text

elements.char: specific form of utility preferences (i.e., mean-variance or mean-variance-skewness or any
elements.label: text

elements.char: other form) to implement this approach. Third, the equilibrium price of volatility provides not
elements.label: text

elements.char: only a more general approach that is very flexible and can also be used for individual securities,
elements.label: text

elements.char: but also serves as a better predictor of future volatility and as an investor fear gauge.

elements.char: Empirically, we generate market state prices from the S&P 500 index options and use them
elements.label: text

elements.char: to price the 49 Fama and French industry portfolio’s volatility. Although our method can be
elements.label: text

elements.char: applied to any traded asset, we focus on industries since understanding the volatility of a par-
elements.label: text

elements.char: ticular industry is crucial for both investors and policy makers [9, 10]. The ex-ante industry
elements.label: text

elements.char: volatility measure constructed in this approach yields better forecasts of realized volatility than
elements.label: text

elements.char: existing approaches and serves as a qualified investor fear gauge. We then demonstrate the
elements.label: text

elements.char: flexibility and generality of our approach by pricing downside and upside opportunity, which
elements.label: text

elements.char: complements the prior work [11–14]. We show that these new upside and downside volatility
elements.label: text

elements.char: measures work well empirically. Finally, we analyze the economic value of volatility timing
elements.label: text

elements.char: using the general equilibrium measures versus existing volatility measures. We show that the
elements.label: text

elements.char: superior forecasting ability of our general equilibrium volatility measure has greater economic
elements.label: text

elements.char: value for investors wishing to manage volatility.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Our paper is related to the recent literature on understanding volatility in a general equilib-
elements.label: text

elements.char: rium framework. As an extension of [15] and [16], Tauchen [17] proposes a consumption-
elements.label: text

elements.char: based general equilibrium model that assumes stochastic consumption. The model generates a
elements.label: text

elements.char: two-factor structure for stock market volatility along with time-varying risk premiums on con-
elements.label: text

elements.char: sumptions and volatility risk, and the leverage effect. In the general equilibrium framework,
elements.label: text

elements.char: Bansal
elements.label: text

elements.char: et al
elements.label: text

elements.char: .[18] demonstrate that besides the cash flow risk and discount rate risk, volatility
elements.label: text

elements.char: risk is an important and separate risk source that cannot be ignored. In contrast to this strand
elements.label: text

elements.char: of literature, we impose no assumptions on consumption dynamics and rely only on state
elements.label: text

elements.char: prices extracted from the options market. The focus of these existing studies is to explain the
elements.label: text

elements.char: stylized facts (e.g., leverage effect, equity risk premium) in the market, while we aim to provide
elements.label: text

elements.char: market participants with an easy and flexible tool to measure and manage the volatilities of
elements.label: text

elements.char: asset portfolios or individual securities.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Our paper is also related to the prior literature on constructing volatility indices based on
elements.label: text

elements.char: options. As long established in the literature, ex-ante risk-neutral volatility can be built upon
elements.label: text

elements.char: the fair value of future variance. Britten-Jones and Neuberger [19] use a replicating strategy to
elements.label: text

elements.char: synthesize a variance swap using options contracts, assuming continuity in the underlying
elements.label: text

elements.char: asset price. Jiang and Tian [20] build on a similar concept by incorporating a jump-diffusion
elements.label: text

elements.char: stochastic volatility model. More recently, Martin [21] proposes a market level volatility index
elements.label: text

elements.char: as the price of squared returns contract and proves it serves as the lower bound for the market
elements.label: text

elements.char: risk premium. Martin and Wagner [22] extend the method of Martin [21] and develop a stock
elements.label: text

elements.char: level volatility index and link it with the expected stock return. Sharing the same spirit of Mar-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tin [21] and the other existing literature, we also treat volatility (or more precisely, the squared
elements.label: text

elements.char: return) as an asset. However, we adopt the general equilibrium approach and are able to con-
elements.label: text

elements.char: struct volatility indices for assets without the need to use traded options. In contrast, Martin
elements.label: text

elements.char: and Wagner [22]’s methodology can only be applied to individual stocks with the availability
elements.label: text

elements.char: of options. Since options either do not exist or are illiquid for most stocks/industry portfolios,
elements.label: text

elements.char: our approach is more general and has a wider application.
elements.label: text

elements.char: Our paper also adds to recent efforts to disentangle the effects of upside and downside uncer-
elements.label: text

elements.char: tainty on asset prices [11, 14] by proposing a new approach for volatility decomposition. One
elements.label: text

elements.char: common approach for decomposing volatility into upside and downside components is to use a
elements.label: text

elements.char: threshold to compute risk-neutral expectations of semi-variances [12, 13, 23]. However, this
elements.label: text

elements.char: approach still depends on the existence of traded options, while our approach does not.
